explain.say: A tsunami is a series of huge waves, usually caused by an earthquake under the sea. When tectonic plates suddenly slip, a large area of seabed is jolted up or down.

faq.a: Most tsunamis are caused by big undersea earthquakes that suddenly lift or drop the seabed. Landslides, volcanic eruptions and, very rarely, meteorite impacts can cause them too.

faq.q: How fast does a tsunami travel?
faq.a: In the deep ocean, about 700 to 800 kilometres per hour, as fast as a jet plane. It slows to tens of kilometres per hour near the coast, but that is still faster than anyone can run.

faq.q: Why does the sea go out before a tsunami?
faq.a: If the trough of the wave arrives first, the sea is pulled back from the shore, sometimes hundreds of metres. It is a warning sign: the crest follows within minutes, so head for high ground at once.
asks: What are the warning signs of a tsunami?

faq.q: Why is a tsunami small in the deep ocean?
faq.a: Its energy is spread through the whole depth of the ocean, several kilometres, so the surface rises less than a metre. Only when the water gets shallow does that energy squeeze into a tall wave.
The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, set off by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra, killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries.

facts: The word tsunami comes from Japanese words meaning harbour wave.
About 80 percent of tsunamis happen in the Pacific Ocean, around the Ring of Fire.

quiz.why: Its energy is spread through the whole ocean depth, so it races along at jet speed with only a small rise at the surface.
